newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Rosneft shake-up to soothe oil investors in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Rosneft shake-up to soothe oil investors in Russia.

text.p: The Russian government reinstated Alexander Putilov as chairman of state oil holding company Rosneft on Tuesday, in a move seen aimed at reassuring foreign partners in potentially huge oil production deals.
Putilov had been relieved of the joint post of Rosneft chairman and president at the end of April by the government, and replaced by former industry minister Yuri Bespalov.

"This decree means that Alexander Putilov has been named chairman of the board of directors, and Yuri Bespalov has been named president," Rosneft first vice-president Rair Simonian said, adding the government decree was signed on Tuesday.

Putilov's speedy return to the ranks of senior Rosneft management followed a weekend of intense talks between Russia's newly-appointed Fuel and Energy Minister Boris Nemtsov and Rosneft's western partners in multi-billion dollar projects.
Foreign company representatives were tight-lipped about what was discussed at the Moscow meetings.
But they said they had made it clear to Nemtsov that changes to Rosneft's management could further delay deals already bogged down in a mire of Russian politics and legislation.
Nemtsov responded by assuring them that changes in Rosneft would not affect their involvement in the projects, Russian news agencies reported.
Yet in a move privately welcomed by western oil company representatives, Putilov was reinstated just two days later.
Some industry analysts said the explanation for Putilov's reinstatement may be straightforward.

"(The) Sakhalin-1 agreement stipulates unchanged company leadership and may force Rosneft to retain Putilov in some leadership position," Moscow-based brokers Renaissance Capital said in a commentary published before Pulikov's reinstatement.
Others said it was because Rosneft was a member of three international oil consortia jointly worth nearly $40 billion, and that Russia could ill afford to put those deals at risk.
Sakhalin-1 is a $15-billion deal to tap reserves off the far east coast of Russia, in which Rosneft has a 17 percent stake.
Rosneft also has a 20 percent share in the $20-billion Timan Pechora Co consortium in the Russian Arctic and a 7.5 percent stake in the $2-billion Caspian Pipeline Consortium.
The two production deals are the kind of mega-projects Russia is keen to start up to arrest the steady decline in oil output, which has roughly halved in the last 10 years.
Russia produced 293 million tonnes of crude oil in 1996, or 5.9 million barrels per day, down around two percent from 1995 levels and the lowest rate for nearly three decades.

Liberal forces in the government argue that exploiting new fields with foreign oil firms is the only way to attract money needed to rejuvenate the ailing sector. Nemtsov, who is also First Deputy Prime Minister, is said to number among them.

But conservative and nationalist parties in the lower house State Duma are blocking the passage of a list of 25 or so new reserves which would be eligible for exploitation under the so-called production sharing agreements.

Duma opposition to foreign participation in Russian oil and an unfavourable tax and tariff regime are the main factors preventing much bigger investments in Russian oil, Western executives based in Moscow said.
Any complications to some of the biggest deals signed so far in the former Soviet Union's energy sector would be an even greater incentive for investors to stay away, they added.
While Putilov's return to the company is likely to allay foreign partners' fears, it does raise fresh doubts over the pace of reform at the company.
Rosneft is due to be privatised later this year and analysts had seen Bespalov's appointment as speeding up this process.
Rosneft was Russia's 10th largest oil group in terms of output last year, with production rising to 13.1 million tonnes (262,000 bpd) from 12.8 million (256,000 bpd) in 1995.
